sections.h2: Which Springfield offices touch a Washington County tax bill?
sections.html:
Three desks in Springfield split the work. The Property Valuation Administrator, or PVA, decides what each parcel is worth. The Sheriff takes money from October until April 15. After that date the County Clerk holds whatever is still open. Nobody at the PVA's counter can accept a payment or change a rate.

Phone numbers to keep handy: 859-336-5420 for the PVA (acreage, assessment, wrong name or address on a bill), 859-336-5400 for the Sheriff (payments, missing bills), and 859-336-5425 for the Clerk (payoff on a prior-year delinquency). Mail and drop-box payments go to 124 East Main Street, Springfield, KY 40069. The Sheriff's tax page has the details.

The bill follows the person listed in PVA records, normally the owner on January 1. If you bought or sold during the year and a bill lands with the wrong household, call the PVA or Sheriff quickly so it gets rerouted.

If you never receive a bill, that does not excuse the tax. Call the Sheriff after the middle of October and ask for a duplicate, then pay before November 1 to keep the 2 percent discount. Owners who mail a check should write the parcel on it and keep the receipt envelope for their records.

The Sheriff cannot take a payment until the bills come over from the Clerk, which happens somewhere between October 1 and mid-October. Plan on a bill in hand around the 15th. Each bill prints four due dates, each with its own dollar amount, under KRS 134.015.

What a Washington County owner pays, by when the Sheriff receives the money
Payment receivedAmount owed
Through November 1Bill minus 2 percent
November 2 through year endPrinted amount
All of JanuaryPrinted amount plus 5 percent
February 1 through April 15Printed amount plus 10 percent

If the state's mailing slips, Revenue can substitute a schedule counted from the mailing date.

sections.h2: Can I use a card or pay online?
sections.html:
No to both. The office explains that card fees would be handed down to taxpayers, so it declines cards, and it runs no web payment system. What it does take is simple.

  • Checks and money orders payable to the Sheriff's Office there; cash only at the window.
  • The yellow postcard stub from your bill, included with any mailed payment, even when one envelope covers several parcels.
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope inside the mailing, if you want a receipt back. Walk-ins are handed one.
  • The outdoor drop box, available after hours.

Postmarks count: an envelope stamped by the due date is honored. Partial payments get mailed back, so a seller cannot park half a bill with the Sheriff and expect the account to clear.

Start with a sit-down at the PVA, then use the clerk's counter for the formal appeal. Public viewing of the roll runs 13 days from the first Monday in May. The clerk wants the written appeal by closing time the next workday. The board of assessment appeals hears cases about a month after that.

  • Bring paper: building and land descriptions, insurance policies, what construction cost, recent listings.
  • Attend the hearing. A no-show gives up any later review by the Kentucky Claims Commission.
  • Hire help only if the person qualifies under Kentucky's representative list, which includes attorneys, CPAs, and appraisers.

Should the board set a figure above yours after bills print, a supplemental bill covers the difference.

The test is age 65 or a total disability, plus living in the house you own. Frankfort fixed the deduction at $49,100 through the 2026 assessment year. The disability route asks for the Social Security notice of award, shown at the PVA office.

The state's rate was 10.6 cents per $100 for 2025, down from 10.9 cents in 2024. Local rates for the county, schools, and districts come on top, so ask the PVA for the full sum on your parcel.

Bring a birth certificate, license, or passport to the PVA. After a sale, tell the office so the credit leaves your old address.

sections.h2: What if taxes are still open when the house sells?
sections.html:
They travel with the land. The state calls the bill the owner's personal debt from the assessment date, and a delinquency lien clings to the parcel for eleven years (KRS 134.420). The title search will show it. Phone the Sheriff about this year and the Clerk about older ones before signing a contract.

At the April 15 handoff the Clerk records a lien, adds 10 percent plus the Sheriff's fee, and starts 1 percent monthly interest. County attorney notices go out. A sale of the certificate can come 90 to 135 days after the handoff, and the purchaser may tack on charges.

For the year of sale, a closing here usually has the seller pay a pro-rated slice for months owned, with the buyer picking up the full bill later. Check the closing statement for how it was split.

sections.h2: Selling a Washington County house with a delinquent bill
sections.html:
An older farmhouse, a house needing repairs, or a parcel with a bill sitting at the Clerk can sell as-is for cash, with the tax cleared at closing. Before you accept an offer, gather the payoff figures: the Sheriff's number for the current year and the Clerk's number for any prior year. Ask for each in writing or note the date and amount you were quoted.

On closing day the title company pays the taxes out of your proceeds and records the release. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, so an open tax bill rarely holds up the closing the way it can with a financed buyer. Confirm with the PVA afterward that the new owner's name is on the roll and that your homestead credit has come off.

Washington County, carved from Nelson County in 1792, has Springfield as its seat, joined by Mackville and Willisburg. The county voted wet in November 2024, ending its status as a dry county with one wet city.

It had 12,368 residents in 2025, up 2.8 percent over 2020. There are 5,325 housing units, and owners occupy 77.6 percent of homes at a median value of $179,200. Median monthly cost with a mortgage is $1,122, and median gross rent is $744, a useful benchmark if you rent out a house. The county issued 26 building permits in 2025, so a seller competes mostly with other resales.

faqs.q: When will my Washington County tax bill arrive?
faqs.a: Expect it around October 15. The Sheriff gets the bills from the Clerk in early to mid October and cannot accept payment before that. If nothing shows up within 10 days of mailing, call the Sheriff for a duplicate.

faqs.q: Does the Washington County Sheriff take credit cards?
faqs.a: No. Payment is by check, money order, or cash in person, and there is no online option, because card fees would be passed to taxpayers.

faqs.q: Whom do I call for prior-year Washington County taxes?
faqs.a: The County Clerk at 859-336-5425 gives payoff amounts for earlier years. Unpaid bills reach the Clerk after April 15 with added penalties and interest.

faqs.q: Do buyer or seller owe the year's tax after a mid-year sale in Washington County?
faqs.a: The contract decides. Many sellers pay a pro-rated share at closing for months owned while the buyer pays the full bill when it comes. Read the settlement statement.

faqs.q: Is there a senior tax break in Washington County?
faqs.a: Yes. Owner-occupants 65 or older, or totally disabled, can deduct $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Apply at the PVA, 859-336-5420.
